paragraphs: Temporal scaling is the ability to produce the same sequence at different speeds. This paper asks how a recurrent neural circuit could support that ability through its dynamics. It uses the mathematics of Lie groups to connect changes in timing with a concrete model of interacting neurons, formulated as a continuous attractor network.

The proposed circuit represents a temporal sequence in its population activity. That representation is equivariant to temporal scaling: changing the timing produces a corresponding transformation of the neural response. A control input implements the transformation, with its gain setting the scaling factor. The spatial offset between the input and the network state supplies the mathematical generator of the transformation.

The authors show that this recurrent circuit can drive a feedforward circuit to produce complex sequences at different speeds, including reversed sequences under negative scaling. Its responses are also consistent with experimental findings. The contribution is an analytical connection between a timing symmetry and a possible neural mechanism for expressing it.
neurips-2023-a-recurrent-neural-circuit-.tldr: A recurrent circuit model connects temporal scaling mathematically to control inputs that change the speed and direction of generated sequences.

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning builds representations from graph data, but recommender systems often train its objective together with the recommendation objective. This paper examines a different arrangement: first learn graph representations without the downstream objective, then adapt them for recommendations. The challenge is connecting what pretraining learns with what the recommendation task needs.

The proposed framework, CPTPP, makes that connection through personalized user prompts. It summarizes user profiles to generate prompts automatically, then combines those prompts with pretrained user embeddings during downstream prompt tuning. Here, the prompts help adapt the learned representation to the recommendation task and reduce the mismatch between the two training stages.

Experiments on three benchmark datasets support CPTPP's effectiveness against leading baselines. A visualization also shows more uniformly distributed user embeddings, which the authors interpret as evidence of better representation of diverse preferences. Together, these findings support personalized prompt tuning as a way to use separate graph contrastive pretraining effectively in recommendation systems.
neurips-2023-an-empirical-study-towards-.tldr: CPTPP adapts separately pretrained graph representations for recommendations using automatically generated, personalized user prompts.

paragraphs: Multi-exit language models save computation by allowing processing to stop before every layer has run. This paper studies whether deliberately modified text can undermine those savings. Its focus is adversarial slowdown: making inputs bypass early exits so that the model must perform more computation.

The authors develop WAFFLE, an attack that produces natural adversarial text, and use it to evaluate three exit mechanisms on GLUE. Across both white-box and black-box settings, the attack substantially reduces their computational savings. Among the mechanisms studied, greater complexity is associated with greater vulnerability. The paper also analyzes recurring linguistic perturbations and compares them with patterns from standard adversarial text attacks.

The defense experiments find that adversarial training does not defeat WAFFLE, while sanitizing inputs with a conversational model can effectively remove its perturbations. These results identify a weakness in the tested efficiency mechanisms and a possible direction for defense. They also motivate evaluating whether early-exit savings survive deliberately difficult inputs.
neurips-2023-bert-lost-patience-won-t-be.tldr: WAFFLE generates text that bypasses early exits and substantially erodes the computational savings of three tested language-model exit mechanisms.

paragraphs: C-Eval is an evaluation suite for testing foundation models' advanced knowledge and reasoning in Chinese. Its motivation is that rapidly improving language models need benchmarks that can reveal capabilities and weaknesses in a Chinese context. The paper contributes both the benchmark and an evaluation of models using it.

The suite contains multiple-choice questions covering 52 disciplines, including humanities, science, and engineering. It spans four educational or professional levels: middle school, high school, college, and professional. An additional subset, C-Eval Hard, collects especially challenging subjects that require advanced reasoning. This structure supports examining performance across subject areas and levels of difficulty.

The evaluation includes both English-oriented and Chinese-oriented models. Among those tested, only GPT-4 exceeds 60% average accuracy, indicating substantial remaining room for improvement on this suite. That finding concerns the models evaluated in the paper. The benchmark is intended to help analyze their strengths and shortcomings and support the development of foundation models for Chinese users.
neurips-2023-c-eval-a-multi-level-multi-.tldr: C-Eval tests Chinese knowledge and reasoning across 52 disciplines and four difficulty levels, revealing substantial gaps among the models evaluated.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether a language model can teach a weaker language model through explanations. Communication has a budget: the teacher can explain only a fraction of examples, and the student should subsequently perform well independently. The research therefore considers whether explanations help, when to provide them, and how to tailor them.

The method builds two few-shot models of the student's behavior. One estimates the benefit of intervening on a particular example, helping the teacher spend its limited budget where explanations are expected to help most. The other supports explanations personalized to that student. The experiments show that targeted intervention improves performance at lower budgets and that personalization outperforms unpersonalized teaching.

Across multiple interaction turns, learning from explained examples also improves performance on later unexplained examples. This suggests that the benefit can extend beyond immediate assistance. The paper additionally demonstrates that deliberately misleading teachers can reduce student performance to random chance, showing that this influence can also damage reasoning.
neurips-2023-can-language-models-teach-t.tldr: Language-model teachers improve student performance by selecting useful interventions and personalizing explanations, including benefits on later unexplained examples.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of selected training examples. This paper develops a certified unlearning algorithm for minimax models, where learning involves coupled minimization and maximization variables. That coupling motivates an update designed for the full minimax problem rather than the single-variable setting emphasized in earlier work.

The algorithm combines a complete Newton update based on a total Hessian with calibrated Gaussian noise. Its analysis measures how close the updated variables are to those obtained by retraining from scratch. This sensitivity calculation determines the noise required for the stated epsilon-delta unlearning certification. The authors also derive population risk guarantees across three cases involving convex-concave and strongly convex-concave losses.

The deletion-capacity result specifies how many samples can be removed while maintaining a desired population risk. With n samples and dimension d, its order is n divided by d to the one-quarter power, improving on the stated differentially private minimax baseline. The rates also match previously established rates for standard statistical learning models.
neurips-2023-certified-minimax-unlearnin.tldr: A minimax-specific Newton update with calibrated Gaussian noise enables certified unlearning with improved deletion capacity over the stated privacy-based baseline.

paragraphs: Equivariant networks make their outputs transform consistently when their inputs undergo specified transformations. This paper develops such networks using Clifford algebra, aiming to construct models with orthogonal and Euclidean symmetries. The approach represents information as multivectors, whose components occupy different grades within the algebra.

The key mathematical result identifies a Clifford group action that preserves both these grades and the geometric product. Consequently, polynomials built from multivectors and their grade projections give equivariant maps. This supplies a systematic way to parameterize neural network layers: the permitted algebraic operations already respect the desired transformation behavior. The construction extends to inner-product spaces of arbitrary dimension.

Using a single core implementation, the authors report state-of-the-art performance on several distinct tasks: a three-dimensional n-body experiment, a four-dimensional Lorentz-equivariant physics experiment, and a five-dimensional convex hull experiment. These results demonstrate the framework's applicability across different dimensions and symmetry settings, alongside the mathematical rules that make its layers equivariant.
neurips-2023-clifford-group-equivariant-.tldr: Clifford algebra supplies symmetry-preserving operations for expressive equivariant neural layers that work across multiple dimensions and tasks.

paragraphs: Online portfolio selection repeatedly allocates investments as data arrives. This paper studies regret guarantees that depend on the observed sequence, allowing the analysis to distinguish difficult data from easier cases. Its contribution is the first small-loss and gradual-variation bounds for this problem, within a setting whose losses lack the usual Lipschitz and smoothness properties.

The proposed algorithms retain sublinear worst-case regret while achieving logarithmic regret when the data is easy in the senses captured by the analysis. Their computation per round is almost linear in the number of investment alternatives. Thus, the results address both adaptation to the data and the computational expense of making each successive decision.

The proofs use new characterizations of logarithmic loss, local norms, and follow-the-regularized-leader methods with self-concordant regularizers. They also introduce an implicit optimistic variant using a log barrier. These tools establish data-dependent guarantees despite the missing global regularity assumptions, broadening the settings in which such adaptive regret analysis is available.
neurips-2023-data-dependent-bounds-for-o.tldr: New portfolio-selection algorithms achieve data-dependent regret guarantees without standard global smoothness assumptions, with faster regret growth on easy data.

paragraphs: Sparse network training seeks small subnetworks that retain the predictive ability of a larger network. This paper focuses on calibration: whether a model's confidence appropriately reflects its predictions' reliability. Preserving accuracy alone does not address overconfident mistakes, especially when inputs come from outside the training distribution.

The proposed method trains an ensemble of sparse subnetworks, or lottery tickets, through distributionally robust optimization. Uncertainty sets guide the tickets toward different data distributions, progressing from easier to harder ones. This encourages diverse subnetworks whose predictions complement one another. The theoretical analysis explains how the robust training procedure guarantees reduced confidence on incorrect predictions.

Across several benchmarks, the ensemble improves calibration without sacrificing accuracy or adding an inference-cost burden in the reported experiments. Tests on out-of-distribution datasets also demonstrate robustness in an open-set setting. The findings support training sparse models with confidence quality as an explicit concern, and show how diversity among tickets can contribute to that goal.
neurips-2023-distributionally-robust-ens.tldr: A distributionally robust ensemble of sparse subnetworks improves reported calibration while preserving accuracy and avoiding additional inference-cost burdens.

paragraphs: Federated learning trains a shared model across nodes that keep their data locally, but exchanging large parameter updates can be expensive. EvoFed reduces that communication by sending fitness values describing local updates. Its central idea is to express an update through comparisons with a shared population of perturbed models.

Every node and the server generate identical perturbed models using synchronized random seeds. Each node measures how close its locally updated model is to each population member and sends those scores. With suitable noise variance and population size, combinations of the perturbed models can closely represent the local update. When the population is much smaller than the parameter count, the score vector is substantially cheaper to transmit.

The server aggregates fitness vectors and distributes the result so all nodes apply the same global update. The paper provides convergence analysis and reports performance comparable to FedAvg with sharply reduced communication across tested settings. These savings come with increased local computation, making the method an explicit exchange of processing work for communication efficiency.
neurips-2023-evofed-leveraging-evolution.tldr: EvoFed exchanges fitness scores over synchronized perturbed models to reduce federated-learning communication at the cost of more local computation.

paragraphs: An optimizer can favor particular solutions even when the training objective does not explicitly select them. This implicit bias helps explain how the choice of optimization method affects the learned classifier. In separable binary classification, gradient-descent methods favor a maximum-margin solution in Euclidean geometry, while other methods can favor margins defined by different geometries.

This paper addresses how quickly generic methods approach their preferred maximum-margin classifiers. Earlier rates for mirror descent and steepest descent were comparatively slow. The authors establish improved, state-of-the-art implicit-bias rates for these methods by changing the mathematical perspective used to analyze their behavior.

The main technique translates an optimization algorithm into an online learning process that solves a regularized bilinear game. Regret bounds for that process then yield faster margin-maximization rates. This shared framework connects several optimization methods and their geometry-dependent preferences. The result concerns the speed of approaching these preferred classifiers, providing a more unified account of implicit bias beyond gradient descent.
neurips-2023-faster-margin-maximization-.tldr: An online-learning game framework yields faster implicit-bias rates for mirror descent and steepest descent toward their maximum-margin classifiers.

paragraphs: This paper studies clients that collaborate through a server while repeatedly choosing actions with uncertain rewards. Rewards follow a linear contextual bandit model, but each client's finite action set can be chosen adversarially and can differ from other clients' sets. The goal is effective collective learning with controlled communication.

The proposed FedSupLinUCB algorithm extends ideas from SupLinUCB and OFUL. Its total regret grows as the square root of d times T, up to polylogarithmic factors, where d is the model dimension and T counts all clients' action selections. This matches the minimax lower bound to those factors. Separate analyses establish communication bounds for synchronized and asynchronous participation.

The authors also extend the method to adapt to reward-noise variance and to tolerate adversarial corruption. The corresponding regret guarantees depend on total noise variance or include an additional term proportional to dimension times the corruption budget. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the analysis, connecting the theoretical guarantees to observed behavior in the tested settings.
neurips-2023-federated-linear-bandits-wi.tldr: FedSupLinUCB achieves near-minimax regret with bounded communication for federated linear bandits with finite adversarial action sets.

paragraphs: In nonconvex optimization, a small gradient can occur at a saddle point as well as near a local minimum. This paper studies how decentralized stochastic optimization can escape saddles efficiently and reach a stronger kind of stationary point. The challenge is obtaining that behavior with stochastic gradients in a decentralized setting.

The proposed algorithm, PEDESTAL, uses only gradient information. A new convergence-analysis framework addresses the difficulties of decentralized stochastic updates and provides a non-asymptotic second-order guarantee. Such a guarantee controls both the gradient and the remaining negative curvature, giving a stronger result than merely reaching a point with a small gradient.

The stated gradient complexity is approximately epsilon to the negative third power, hiding polylogarithmic factors, for the specified approximate second-order stationarity target. This matches leading centralized results or decentralized first-order results. Experiments on synthetic matrix sensing and real-data matrix factorization validate the method's performance. The contribution is efficient, finite-computation saddle escape with a stronger optimization guarantee in the decentralized setting.
neurips-2023-finding-local-minima-effici.tldr: PEDESTAL uses stochastic gradients to escape saddles in decentralized optimization with a finite-computation second-order stationarity guarantee.

paragraphs: Directional Stimulus Prompting guides a black-box language model using hints generated specifically for each input. A smaller, tunable policy model produces these auxiliary prompts, such as keywords that should appear in a summary. The large model receives the guidance through its input, allowing behavior to be adapted without directly tuning its parameters.

The policy model can learn through supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning using rewards from the large model's outputs. This makes prompt generation an optimization problem: learn which instance-specific clues lead to desirable responses. The paper evaluates the framework on summarization, dialogue generation, and chain-of-thought reasoning.

The experiments report consistent improvements for the tested models with limited labeled data. Using 80 MultiWOZ dialogues, the method improves ChatGPT's performance by a relative 41.4%, matching or exceeding some fully supervised methods. Generated reasoning prompts also improve InstructGPT's accuracy over general human-written and automatically engineered prompts. These findings support learning personalized guidance for individual inputs.
neurips-2023-guiding-large-language-mode.tldr: A small trainable model learns input-specific hints that improve black-box language-model outputs without directly tuning the large model.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often treats the interval between observations as fixed. For continuous-time systems, that interval can sometimes be chosen. This paper asks how the choice affects policy evaluation: estimating the value of a given policy from a limited amount of data. It analyzes Monte Carlo evaluation in linear-quadratic regulator systems.

The analysis separates two sources of error. Approximation error comes from representing continuous behavior at discrete times, while statistical error reflects estimation from finite data. These errors respond differently to temporal resolution. Their interaction produces a trade-off, with an optimal resolution for a given data budget rather than an unconditional benefit from choosing finer timing.

For the analyzed LQR setting, managing temporal resolution provably improves policy-evaluation efficiency with finite data. Numerical LQR simulations demonstrate the trade-off, and experiments on nonlinear continuous-control benchmarks show it empirically as well. The distinction matters: the theoretical guarantee is established for LQR systems, while the broader control results provide experimental evidence of the same phenomenon.
neurips-2023-managing-temporal-resolutio.tldr: Choosing observation timing balances approximation and statistical errors, enabling more efficient finite-data policy evaluation in the analyzed LQR setting.

paragraphs: Millimetre-wave radar offers a cost-effective, non-intrusive way to sense human activity, with better privacy protection than traditional camera systems. Its reflected radio signals, however, make the resulting measurements more prone to noise. MiliPoint addresses the research need this creates: data for developing deep learning methods that work effectively with radar point sets.

The paper introduces a large, openly available point-cloud dataset for human activity recognition. The authors report that it is larger than existing datasets, represents a wider variety of human actions, and covers all three key tasks in human activity recognition. This combination gives researchers a shared resource for studying the sensor across a broader range of activities.

The work also establishes baseline point-based neural networks on the dataset, including DGCNN, PointNet++, and PointTransformer. These baselines provide reference results for future method development. The contribution brings together data and initial evaluations so researchers can investigate how point-set learning handles the opportunities and noisy measurements of mmWave radar.
neurips-2023-milipoint-a-point-cloud-dat.tldr: MiliPoint provides an open mmWave radar point-cloud dataset and neural-network baselines for studying human activity recognition.

paragraphs: This paper learns representations of neural network architectures themselves. Such representations can predict properties like accuracy or latency without carrying out the full training or deployment procedure. The authors aim to support both cell-structured architectures and entire networks within one Transformer-based representation model.

NAR-Former V2 first treats an architecture as a graph and converts it into a sequence using a tokenizer. It then incorporates the inductive representation-learning capability associated with graph neural networks into a modified Transformer. Additional architectural changes improve its handling of graph structure. Together, these choices are intended to help the model represent networks and generalize to previously unseen architectures.

For whole-network latency prediction on NNLQP, the method substantially outperforms the graph-based NNLP method. For cell-structured accuracy prediction on NASBench101 and NASBench201, it performs comparably to leading approaches. The results support the proposed design across these two representation settings, showing that a modified Transformer can be useful for both architectural scales and their associated prediction tasks.
neurips-2023-nar-former-v2-rethinking-tr.tldr: NAR-Former V2 combines graph-informed design with Transformers to represent both network cells and entire architectures for property prediction.

paragraphs: NU-MCC reconstructs three-dimensional objects from a single RGB-D input, which combines color and depth. It addresses two weaknesses identified in MCC: expensive decoding when many spatial query points are used and difficulty recovering fine geometric details. The proposed changes target both computation and the representation of the reconstructed surface.

A neighborhood decoder introduces center points that summarize input visual features. Each query attends only to a small nearby group, reducing decoding work and enabling the use of finer-scale visual features. The second change replaces MCC's occupancy representation with a repulsive unsigned distance function. This representation improves reconstruction quality and produces more complete surfaces than standard unsigned distance functions, which can leave holes.

The experiments report improved single-view reconstruction quality alongside faster execution. On CO3D-v2, NU-MCC outperforms MCC by 9.7% in F1-score and runs more than five times faster. The stated result shows that the two changes can improve surface recovery while also addressing the computational burden of querying a detailed three-dimensional representation.
neurips-2023-nu-mcc-multiview-compressiv.tldr: NU-MCC combines local decoding with a repulsive distance representation to improve single-view 3D reconstruction quality and speed.

paragraphs: Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization seeks models that perform well across distributions close to the observed data. It handles geometric uncertainty, such as localized movement of data points, but arbitrary outliers can badly distort the distance it uses. This paper develops a framework that explicitly includes both kinds of uncertainty.

The proposed uncertainty set combines Wasserstein perturbations with total-variation contamination, allowing an epsilon fraction of the data to be corrupted arbitrarily. The authors derive minimax-optimal excess-risk bounds that separately account for these two sources of risk. This makes the robustness target reflect both shifts in ordinary observations and contamination by potentially extreme observations.

A strong duality result enables tractable convex reformulations and efficient computation. When the loss depends only on low-dimensional features, the analysis also removes certain dimension dependencies that cannot be avoided in the general case. Regression and classification experiments validate the theory. The work connects an expanded uncertainty model with both statistical guarantees and a computational route for solving the resulting problem.
neurips-2023-outlier-robust-wasserstein-.tldr: An outlier-robust Wasserstein framework handles both geometric shifts and arbitrary contamination with optimal risk bounds and tractable reformulations.

paragraphs: A language model reasoning over supplied context can be distracted by facts that are valid but irrelevant to the current question. RECKONING addresses this problem by encoding contextual knowledge into model parameters before asking the question. The approach uses a temporary adaptation of the model to make that knowledge available for subsequent reasoning.

Training has two nested loops. The inner loop rapidly updates a copy of the weights through backpropagation to encode the supplied knowledge. The outer loop teaches the model to reproduce that knowledge and answer reasoning questions using the updated weights. This trains both the knowledge-encoding process and the ability to reason from what it stores.

Across three multi-hop reasoning datasets, RECKONING improves performance over in-context reasoning by up to 4.5%. It also generalizes better to longer reasoning chains absent from training and is more robust to distractors. When multiple questions concern the same knowledge, it is computationally more efficient, making the reuse of encoded knowledge a particularly relevant setting.
neurips-2023-reckoning-reasoning-through.tldr: RECKONING learns to encode supplied knowledge into adapted model weights, improving tested reasoning performance and resistance to distractors.

paragraphs: An agent learning through free play needs a reason to explore before it has a specific task. This paper proposes rewarding regularity: the creation of structure and order. Inspired by child development, the authors hypothesize that this motivation can draw exploration toward useful activities that simple uncertainty-based rewards do not favor.

Their formulation, Regularity as Intrinsic Reward, or RaIR, can be incorporated into model-based reinforcement learning. In a synthetic environment, pursuing the reward produces a variety of structured patterns. In a robotic environment with multiple objects, the authors combine RaIR with epistemic uncertainty, so free play is guided by both regularity and the model's uncertainty about its knowledge.

During this robotic free play, the agent autonomously constructs towers and other regular arrangements. The resulting experience leads to substantially better zero-shot performance on downstream assembly tasks. These findings support regularity as a useful complement to uncertainty in the tested environments, connecting the structure of exploratory behavior with the usefulness of what the agent learns.
neurips-2023-regularity-as-intrinsic-rew.tldr: Rewarding structure during free play encourages regular object arrangements and improves tested zero-shot robotic assembly performance.

paragraphs: Hierarchical reinforcement learning organizes planning across multiple levels of abstraction. Experiments have suggested that this can reduce the experience needed to learn, but explaining those gains theoretically remains difficult. This paper studies the sample complexity of a particular class of goal-conditioned hierarchical algorithms to make that benefit more precise.

The authors derive a lower bound on the number of samples required within the considered class. The bound helps quantify the benefit of hierarchical decomposition and informs a simple Q-learning-type algorithm that uses such decompositions. This links a theoretical account of learning requirements to an algorithmic design, rather than leaving hierarchy solely as an empirical choice.

Experiments examine the proposed algorithm on hierarchical n-rooms tasks and Gymnasium's Taxi task. The n-rooms construction allows task complexity to vary over multiple orders of magnitude, supporting evaluation across a wide range of difficulty. The findings provide a step toward quantifying how hierarchical decomposition improves sample requirements relative to monolithic learning within the studied framework.
neurips-2023-sample-complexity-of-goal-c.tldr: A sample-complexity lower bound helps quantify hierarchical reinforcement-learning benefits and guides a simple hierarchy-aware Q-learning algorithm.

paragraphs: Translation averaging reconstructs absolute translations from pairwise relative directions in three-dimensional vision. This paper studies sensitivity: how small uncertainty in those directions affects the recovered translations. A solution can be unique yet still be highly unstable under small changes to its inputs, making sensitivity a separate concern from uniqueness or outlier rejection.

The authors first examine how perturbing relative directions affects the estimated scales associated with them. They then define conditioning for translation averaging using only the input directions and give a sufficient criterion for good conditioning. An efficient algorithm identifies and removes combinations of directions that cause instability while preserving uniqueness of the solution.

The paper demonstrates the analysis within global structure-from-motion pipelines. Filtering ill-conditioned direction sets reduces translation errors, increases the number of triangulated three-dimensional points, and speeds up bundle adjustment in the reported results. The contribution is therefore both diagnostic and practical: it characterizes unreliable input configurations and provides a way to improve reconstruction by filtering them.
neurips-2023-sensitivity-in-translation-.tldr: Conditioning analysis identifies unstable direction combinations in translation averaging and supports filtering that improves reported 3D reconstructions.

paragraphs: Explaining an individual action does not necessarily reveal which moments determine a reinforcement-learning agent's final reward. StateMask targets that longer-term question. It seeks the states that matter most to the final outcome, providing an explanation of performance across a sequence rather than only a justification for isolated decisions.

The method learns a masking network that blinds the target agent at selected steps and forces random actions there. It aims to do this without compromising performance. By learning where such substitutions can occur while retaining the reward, the method identifies which parts of the interaction are critical. The authors provide a theoretical design ensuring that the masked agent performs similarly to the original.

Across several popular reinforcement-learning environments, StateMask achieves higher explanation fidelity than existing explainers in the reported evaluations. The paper also demonstrates improved utility for launching adversarial attacks and patching policy errors. These applications connect its explanations to interventions that test or improve the agent's behavior.
neurips-2023-statemask-explaining-deep-r.tldr: StateMask identifies reward-critical states by learning where an agent can take random actions while retaining similar performance.

paragraphs: Urban prediction models can benefit from knowledge that connects different parts of a city. Existing urban knowledge graphs are often built for individual tasks and unavailable publicly, limiting their reuse. UUKG provides a shared dataset intended to support knowledge-enhanced prediction across multiple urban tasks involving space and time.

The dataset contains graphs for two metropolises, with millions of relationship triplets connecting entities such as boroughs, points of interest, and road segments. Qualitative and quantitative analyses reveal higher-order structures, including hierarchies and cycles. These patterns provide potential information beyond isolated relationships between pairs of entities.

The authors evaluate 15 embedding methods on knowledge-graph completion, then integrate the resulting representations into nine spatiotemporal models across five prediction tasks. This creates benchmarks for comparing knowledge-enhanced predictions under different settings. The results also highlight the potential of embedding methods that account for higher-order structure. Publicly available data and code make the work a resource for further study of urban graphs and their predictive value.
neurips-2023-uukg-unified-urban-knowledg.tldr: UUKG provides large urban knowledge graphs and benchmarks showing their potential to support prediction across multiple city tasks.
